notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00539.opp-gr: Line 11 (section 9): the printed text reads 'τοῦ καλοῦ τος', evidently a mangled 'παρόντος' ('being present'), which the following 'ἀπόντος' ('being absent') requires; translated so. Line 15 (section 12): 'ἡδονῆς ἐκοινώνησέ σοι' ('share pleasure with you') seems to be a deliberate double meaning, as do the plurals 'whom we have' (section 3) and 'we had her' (section 11), which hint at the rumour.

Section 18: the sentence beginning "Yet I claim" may be meant as a further indignant question or a sarcastic concession; the sense is uncertain. Section 25: the comparison of the father who kills with one who "has brought to trial" takes κρίναντος in the sense of prosecuting; it could also mean "judged". Section 29: the printed text has stray letters (εῖ εἶ) after γυναῖκα, omitted here as a scanning error. Section 32: the poets who make Rumour a god are not named; compare Hesiod, Works and Days 763-764. Section 34: the words ἡγοῦμαι καὶ ἀποθανεῖν are an editor's supplement, marked in the Greek with angle brackets and rendered here in square brackets.

36.1: the genitive in ἄλλο τι φαίνεται τοῦ ... πάθους is awkward and the text may be defective; rendered as 'because of the passion'. 37.1: τιμᾷ ('honours') is odd in context, where the sense seems to be that she is attended by each man in turn; the text may be corrupt. 44.1: 'give [money]' is an inference from δοῦναι δυναμένους, which has no object; 'being trusted' presumably means trusted by husbands. 44.2: φανέντ᾿ ὃς ποθὲν μοιχοῦ is corrupt as printed; translated as if φανέντος ποθὲν μοιχοῦ. The sense of οὐδὲν ἔσται μοι παίδων αἰδεσιμώτερον is unclear in context; it may mean that no regard for anyone's sons will restrain him, and the text may be sound or not. Scanning errors corrected without change of sense: ἔνα for ἵνα, 0) for ὦ.

nodes.text: XXXIX.
There was a rumour that the father was sleeping with his son's wife. The father made a law permitting sons to be killed untried. The son also makes a law, permitting adulterers to be killed untried.
[The declamation].

Since my father says that he has taken thought through his law for the good conduct of the young, accept from me too a law that can make adulterers more moderate for us. And you must consider that this law too is being proposed by my father. For the man who has educated me in everything else, and has so formed my mind that I now even undertake to introduce laws on behalf of marriage, how could he not reasonably be thought responsible for what I am doing today?

And one might well wonder at this: that when he ought to be fighting at his son's side, praising the law and working with me to see it enacted, he has come to oppose me, as though he were being wronged or were not going to share the glory with me, and this although he has had a share in all that is mine, small and great alike.

Now I have had it in mind for a long time, men of the jury, to propose this law, ever since my father brought into the house for us this wife whom we have; but hesitation, which does much harm to the young in many places, consumed a long time for me in delay. But when I saw that my father by his law had deprived the jurors of authority over sons and was handing over their slaughter to their parents, then I too was at last moved to bring into the open what I had long wished to do and kept putting off. For this law, which you would rightly have passed for the sake of chastity even if no such law had been introduced before, I thought you would accept the more readily since it gives husbands against adulterers what you have given parents against sons.

4. Now in other respects I trust that the law will be thought sound, but I fear one thing only, men of the jury: that the fact that its proposer is young and a son, while its opponent is older and a father, may harm what has been correctly drafted. But if you had not already seen many older men committing the faults of the young, and many younger men finding what is needed far better than many of their elders, you would do well to make age the judge; but since natures are stronger than the number of one's years, what wonder is it if a father is carried away from what is proper and a son says something better?

Now if my father had not created a worse reputation for me through his law, I would at once be trying to show that this law of mine is beneficial; but since some of you were looking at me while he was legislating, and some, naturally enough, were visited by the thought that this man has evidently found his son wicked towards him, wishes to kill him himself, and has been striving for this, not to help other fathers but to gratify himself with the slaughter of a foul son, come, let me make my defence to you, using my father as a witness.

6. You used to send me, father, when I was quite young, to my teachers. Did I incur any blame there of the sort most boys incur? Did I disgrace you by my conduct? Certainly not. After that, when my mother died (while she lived you would never have made this law, for she would have stopped you), was I in a hurry to marry? Did I speak to you about a wife, as someone might who was dragging himself away from living with you? Not that either.

No, the one urging me towards marriage was this man, men of the jury, saying: 'We need a wife, my boy, a wife who will take care of the household, and put an end to the grief for your mother by filling her place for me and somehow restoring the house to its former order.' And I, blushing, said that these things would be just as he himself wished, but that perhaps we should not marry so quickly, nor while still in mourning prepare banquets, set out mixing bowls, invite guests together and sing the wedding song. He said that I was talking nonsense, for she who was to take her place must come in at once.

I gave way, men of the jury, and agreed, although I knew perfectly well that this thing, marriage, has been for many people the cause of many great evils. For adulterers, father, against whom I am now legislating, countless men, even ones you would not have expected, have laid hands on another man's bed, and those whose duty it was to guard it have often themselves corrupted it. | And I received this fear from the poets while still young, and why should I recount it to you? For you know what they say. But nevertheless I chose to take my risk in the uncertainty of the future rather than fight against my father's desire.

So when it had been decided that I should marry, it cannot be said of what followed either that I caused this man any grief. For it was not that he wanted to take one woman and I another, nor did I come into strife with him over these things or struggle against him; I asked only this much: 'Is she from chaste people, father, and has she practised chastity?' For I knew, men of the jury, that when this virtue is present, both a wife's poverty and her ugliness are a light matter, and whatever else one might name, but when it is absent, neither wealth nor beauty nor birth contributes even a small part towards consolation.

For what good could one set against so great an evil? And by what could one bear so terrible a blow? It would be dreadful even if it could stay hidden, but as it is, it is done and talked about at the same time: the first to notice it informs another, he a third, and this one yet another. And so the story reaches the marketplace and is sung there.

For these reasons, men of the jury, I mentioned none of the other things and asked only to learn about her chastity. But he, looking fiercely at me, said, 'I have been the examiner of these matters, I know the girl. Have no fear about one who pleases me.' Hearing this I kept quiet and was speechless, and thought that I must marry according to this man's judgement. We took the bride, we brought her home, we had her. Did I do anything wrong after this, then? Let him say so.

12. And not only of my own conduct, but also of my wife's conduct towards him I am ready to make an examination. Did she not look after us both alike? Did she not take thought for your needs just as for mine, food, clothing, bed? Did she not share pleasure with you, | as my mother did before? Did she not come to you and attend you when you came in from outside? Did she not see you off when you went out, praying that you would soon return? Did she not make you forget my mother's death by doing everything that my mother had done?

And while this was going on, father, did I ever reproach or cry out against my wife, as one who did not put my interests first but divided herself exactly between me and you? Why, if anyone, slave or free, comes forward and testifies against me, write a law against sons even harsher than this one, if that is possible.

14. So when I have thus submitted to your plans and have made myself master of nothing, but have simply yielded everything to you, what is the reason for this fine law? Why do you give these men cause to suspect that there is some war in our house requiring swift slaughter, which must be done before anyone knows why?

15. But if not when you proposed the law, at least now that you have proposed it, expose my wickedness, define the charges, and do not let those standing around think different things. Or do you not suppose that many of these men, some each to himself, others to one another, are saying many such things as I could never utter? For things that are unbearable even to hear, how could I bring myself to speak them? Except that I will say this much: some of these men think that I have done wrong and by offending have roused you to this law, while others perhaps say that I am being wronged and am unfortunate and am hated for that reason.

Let us remove the suspicions of the crowd by stating your son's misdeeds. But you do not wish to? Is this not, then, defence enough for me? And it was for this reason, with the law already in place, that I have used these words to you, men of the jury, so that from this too you might learn my reasonableness | and that I have nowhere opposed my father's impulses. For if I, who am to live amid such great fears, did not dare to break into speech, what else have I not borne in silence?

So when I heard this man reading out a law depriving sons of a trial and claiming that the city would not otherwise be well run, and saw you tolerating it, I thought that the moment had come for me too to propose a law, which, as I said at the beginning, I had long wished to propose and somehow had not dared. And consider, by Zeus, whether it is not a fine law, fitting for the city and in agreement with the other [laws] concerning marriage.

18. To the man who catches an adulterer with his wife, it says, it shall be permitted to kill the outrager at once. But my father is indignant and has come to speak against it. Why, father, have I no share in making laws? Do I go about the city disenfranchised, and must I bow my head to the ground? Yet I claim the greatest privileges for myself and I draft laws.

Whether anyone else has driven me out of my freedom of speech, I do not know, but under the laws of the constitution I have not yet suffered this. So I am legislating when I am permitted to do so, and I am drafting on a matter that concerns me, and no one could say that I am seizing on another's business, as, for example, if I were proposing laws about ships or cavalry or hoplites or tribute or the city wall or resident aliens or taxes, I would reasonably be thought to be dragging to myself the business of generals and orators and of older men generally. But it is fitting for us younger men to draft laws against adulterers.

And there is nothing surprising in this. For we live with young wives, father. And if they also surpass others in appearance, as our wife does, since my father took this too into consideration, so that the wife's body might delight the eyes of the man living with her, then the man who has such a wife has a natural reason for setting every guard around her beauty. So not only am I permitted, but I am also proposing a law about what most concerns me. And whoever knows our affairs exactly, as I think many do, praises my zeal as well.

21. First, then, see how clear and just the law is. Let the man who catches an adulterer, it says, not bring him to trial, but slaughter him himself. What is clearer than this? And indeed, by saying "adulterer" it simply includes every adulterer, whether he is young or not young, whether unknown or known, whether a close acquaintance or not, whether from outside or from within the household, and it has made no exception at all, not of family, not of fortune, not of age. What is more just than this?

And that the law is beneficial is surely clear to everyone. For I know that armies save cities, and that the greatest of prizes, legitimate children, makes those who go out to war brave. But if someone makes the birth of these children suspect to me, father, he makes a poor hoplite of the man fighting for them. So this law, which upholds chastity, guards the city.

23. I wonder, too, what argument my father has found in coming here to block the law. For he has lost that strong argument, that no one ought to die untried in a democracy. How? None of the ancient laws has made a father master of his children's lives; rather, to beat them, to drive them from the table, not to speak to them, to distress them with harsh words and the like has been granted to a father, and for these things there is no need of jurors or votes, but to kill, to destroy and to cut down a young man who has not faced a charge in public, has not obtained jurors, and has not had his turn to speak, was thought terrible, impious and far from democracy. And why do I speak of slaughter? Under the ancient laws a son will not undergo even disownment untried. Will he who could not be deprived even of his father's property without a trial die in ignorance of the charge that brings his death?

And why does the father actually avoid a court? someone might say. For the charge, surely, falls on the one who will pay the penalty, not the one who will exact it. State the charge, it says, prove it, see him pay the penalty. But you state nothing so serious. Stop your raging. The laws have not surrendered the city's youth to the seething anger of fathers, knowing that anger often overpowers reason.

But it is shameful for fathers to recount their sons' offences. Does a slaughter, then, become evidence of anything good? And in court the son will die thought guilty only of the wrong he has done, but if no trial has taken place, there is nothing that he will not be thought to have done. For those who do not know the real charge must guess at everything. And so a father who has killed is more wretched than one who has brought to trial.

It was for these reasons that the ancient laws established a trial and did not deprive citizens of what they granted to household slaves; at any rate, you will not kill any slave, father, untried, but all the same you have shown those ancient provisions, confirmed by long time, to be mere nonsense, and you have made fathers the slaughterers of their sons. No one opposes your law. Let it prevail along with the other laws on homicide, or, if you like, let it even be praised above them. This very thing, however, has made a path for the law against adulterers. And it is easier for me to propose this one than it was for you to propose that earlier one, in proportion as I am looking to a precedent as I draft, while you were demanding the newest thing of all. So when sons are to die untried, will the same not be imposed on an adulterer?

27. For what prevents us, it says, from bringing the man caught to trial? I will answer you on this, father. First, it is hard for the victim of so great an evil to bear the sight and to hold back a right hand urged on to murder by the outrage before his eyes. Second, facts have often been defeated by words in the courts, and the adulterer has seemed chaste and the wronged man a false accuser. For there are many things that often help the accused: experience in affairs, the defendant's reputation, a crowd of advocates. And grey hair and age have before now rescued someone; and the man of whom you would not say, seeing him, that he commits such offences, this man commits adultery, and with the very woman you would not suspect.

For many wrongs are incredible to hear of, yet they are done. And if something of the kind happens even now, one may investigate. Tragedies, at any rate, are full of astonishing evils. And these must not be thought to have stopped in those times. For since nature is the same, it is surely likely that the same things are dared too.

Does the adulterer need a court? What then if the prosecutor is the younger man? What if the adulterer is of an age with his father? Do you not think that some will rebuke him, some will disbelieve him, and some will urge that the man be let off? And what if those who are to give evidence value the adulterer above the injured man? Must there not, on top of the misfortune concerning his wife, also be the penalty for false accusation? So let me, by Zeus, father, propose the law, and stop causing me pain, since you are distressing me now, but once it has been ratified you will do so no longer.

But do you blame me for drafting it? You have been the cause of these things for me, through my wife. For if you had not admired her to me or praised her beauty or compelled me to marry, I would have been free of these present worries and fears. As it is, marriage and fear have made me a legislator. Or from what source do you think these many adulteries are dared? Is it not because adulterers have ways of slipping out of trials? This evil must at last be made as small as possible, and there is need of this law to help those who are married and to check this unbearable outrage.

31. And we who live in the city will gain another very great benefit, men of the jury. For if greater care is taken over women, we will also shut the mouths of these people who enjoy slandering. For at present they fill the marketplace with such talk: so-and-so [has had] so-and-so's wife. And if anyone disbelieves it, there is an oath at once. And the man who has heard it, instead of restraining the speaker, becomes another's teacher, and the matter advances and becomes rumour.

Then the poets harm us more than these, having made Rumour a god and bearing witness for the slanderers. We will stop these people, father, through the law. For they will no longer seem to be saying credible things when the outraged husbands stand over adulterers with the sword. So let the law by all means help the city, and we will enjoy our share of it.

33. But many, it says, will lure their enemies to their homes by a trick and kill them, falsely claiming that they are adulterers. And who is so foolish or so ill-starred, father, as to be willing to pay a greater penalty than he exacts? Or do you think it an equal penalty to die and to be outraged through one's wife? Do you not know that the one has no sensation of anything after the blow, while the other must live in disgrace?

What are you saying? Will a chaste man die as an adulterer? And how will the killer live, thought to have suffered such things? For to me, father, this seems the most unbearable thing of all. But you do not think so. Nothing is so terrible: not confiscation of property, not mutilation of the body, not the deaths of children, not exile and wandering in foreign lands, not the executioner, not hemlock, not being thrown out unburied. It is for this reason above all that I hate tyrannies, because they consider such outrages their greatest pleasure. This, whether done or merely believed, [I consider] the ultimate calamity, [and] I would accept [death] rather than spread over my house the reputation of an adultery that has not happened.

35. So take heart about the chaste, father. As for those who are not so, let us not be too concerned for them, nor make up fears, so that we do not force someone to say: "You think that a man who is no adulterer will die through enmity, but do you not think that an excellent son will die as a wicked one through the wickedness of a father?" What if the father has wronged his son and hates him for this very reason, because he knows that he has been wronged? Shall we give him the power to kill?

Do you not see even now some men harsh toward their own? What, then, do we suppose they will be once impunity is given? For do not imagine, men of the jury, that nature is a sufficient bond. It prevails for the most part, but when the diseases of the soul grow stronger, it is cut through, and the father appears as something else because of the passion that compels his soul.

If you want the law you have enacted to stand firm for you, yield to this one too. For by contending you unsettle that one as well. Have you then found the wife guilty of some incontinence? And have you, father, found your son guilty of some depravity? Yet still you legislate in suspicion of the future. So it is unobjectionable for me too to think the future deserving of greater and less laborious care, since as things stand the wife is a very laborious business for those who guard her. For she honours now me, now him. For we do not go out together, men of the jury. No, my father has devised a clever scheme concerning the wife. He goes to the marketplace himself while I stay at home, and he spends his time at home while I walk about in the marketplace, so that the little woman is with either me or him, and if her husband is away, she has her father-in-law as a guard in place of her husband.

But for this very reason, surely, it is right for this law to be ratified, so that my father may at last stop sitting beside the wife, worrying and toiling and neglecting public affairs. For this law will at once release him from the wife, being established as a sufficient guardian of chastity.

How our mother ought still to be alive, men of the jury! Then none of what is now happening would be taking place. For what need would I have of a law, when her eyes were enough to keep guard? But now, since she has died, I have come to this: I am legislating, and freeing both my father and myself from our present troubles.

Come then, father, released from affairs at home, give yourself wholly to public affairs and the wife to the law. Make your political career continuous and consider that you have become a different man today. Go before the people, give your opinions in the council, serve as an ambassador, serve as a general, make some fine journey abroad. You do care for my wife; I know it, and all these men know well that you have far surpassed other fathers-in-law in your conduct toward her. But having won enough reputation from that, acquire the reputation that comes from greater things, especially since you have also furnished the city with a son able to draft laws.

I will assist you in your public activities, not parting from you even a little, going out from home with you, coming home with you, all but grown together with you, serving this sweetest of slaveries, if indeed I seem to you to be without fault and you do not become the first of fathers to use the law against me.

42. And indeed, stand up and say before these men what I must do and what I must not do to escape your right hand. And if I do not obey in everything that is honourable, kill me. Must I not mention estates? I will not mention them. Must I not touch money? I will not touch it. Must I not give orders to the household slaves? I will not give orders. Must I put up with wearing a shabby cloak? I will put up with it. Must I endure going hungry? I will endure it. Be silent? I will not utter a sound. Sleep on the ground? I will do this. All these things I will do to please you. And you will not see me insolent about them. But let me be allowed to hate adulterers and to draft laws against them.

And my father will say that in other respects too I have become more cheerful and not unpleasant to be with. For now he often reproaches me: "Why do you look so sullen, child? Why do you look like those in mourning?" At that time I said nothing, but now I will tell you: wishing to enact this law against adulterers, father, but always delaying, I was weighed down, and as if in labour pains I ached in my heart. But if it should be ratified today, and you should give way and bear with this too, you will see the downcast man smiling, you will see the man who cowered looking like a free man.

A certain reasoning made me this way; a foolish one, as you would say, but it did make me so. I thought that the old law was too feeble in its anger against adulterers, so that even the many were being drawn toward other men's marriages, some being able to give [money], others being trusted. After this law you will no longer see me as I was before, but as is fitting for a man who has sufficient confidence about his wife.

45. You, father, proclaim to these young men standing around: "Children, beware the anger of your fathers," and I too will make a counter-proclamation to old and young, to foreigner and citizen, to son and father: "Be chaste, and shudder at the husband's right hand, since the same bed will receive both the outrage and the slaughter." I will be the first to live carrying a sword, and whomever I catch, I will use the sword, and nothing will command more reverence from me than my children. Rather, having sharpened my sword, I will take my rest holding it, and if an adulterer appears from anywhere, I will ask my father to help.
